# AMR-SD: Asymmetric Meta-Reflective Self-Distillation for Token-Level Credit Assignment

###### Abstract

The alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) for complex reasoning
heavily relies on Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR).
However, standard algorithms like GRPO apply sequence-level rewards
uniformly to all tokens, creating a severe credit-assignment bottleneck.
While on-policy self-distillation attempts to resolve this by
conditioning a self-teacher on privileged contexts, direct exposure to
raw oracle solutions often induces over-conditioned teacher
distributions, implicit answer leakage, and late-stage training
collapse. To overcome these limitations, we propose Asymmetric
Meta-Reflective Self-Distillation (AMR-SD). Instead of conditioning
directly on raw reference traces, AMR-SD inserts a reflection
bottleneck: it compresses diagnostic signals—from verifier outcomes,
peer rollouts, or reference feedback—into concise, self-generated
Socratic hints and critiques. Furthermore, we introduce Causal
Information Gain (CIG) with an asymmetric, ReLU-gated threshold to
translate these reflections into sparse, highly precise token-level
advantage modulations. Combined with temporal annealing, this mechanism
preserves the base environmental reward while filtering out
distributional noise. Experiments across scientific, mathematical, and
tool-use benchmarks demonstrate that AMR-SD significantly outperforms
existing baselines, achieving robust long-horizon stability and
successfully preventing late-stage collapse.

## 1 Introduction

The alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) for complex reasoning
heavily relies on Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
(RLVR) [Yu et al. (2025)](#bib.bib28); [Wu et al. (2025)](#bib.bib27).
Standard policy gradient algorithms, such as Group Relative Policy
Optimization (GRPO) [Guo et al. (2025)](#bib.bib4); [Schulman et al.
(2017)](#bib.bib14), efficiently estimate advantages from sparse
sequence-level outcomes. However, GRPO applies a uniform advantage
scalar to all tokens within a rollout. This creates a severe
credit-assignment bottleneck: critical logical deductions and
superficial stylistic choices receive identical reward signals,
hampering the optimization of reasoning tasks [Yang et al.
(2026b)](#bib.bib21); [Li et al. (2026d)](#bib.bib26); [Xie et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib25); [Li et al. (2026b)](#bib.bib24).

To resolve this credit-assignment bottleneck, offline Supervised
Fine-Tuning (SFT) offers dense supervision but suffers from severe
train-test distribution shifts. To bridge the gap between RL’s on-policy
exploration and SFT’s dense supervision, the community turned to
On-Policy Distillation (OPD) [Agarwal et al. (2024)](#bib.bib7). While
highly effective [Xiao et al. (2026)](#bib.bib13); [Team et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib15), maintaining an external teacher incurs prohibitive
computational overhead. Consequently, On-Policy Self-Distillation
emerged, utilizing the model itself as the teacher conditioned on
privileged information (e.g., ground-truth solutions)
(Figure [1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ AMR-SD: Asymmetric Meta-Reflective Self-Distillation for Token-Level Credit Assignment")) [Zhao
et al. (2026)](#bib.bib10); [Hübotter et al. (2026)](#bib.bib2);
[Shenfeld et al. (2026)](#bib.bib30); [Zhang et al. (2026)](#bib.bib29).
However, directly forcing a conditionally independent student to match a
conditionally dependent teacher introduces information asymmetry. The
student blindly imitates confident reasoning without accessing the
underlying context, leading to privileged information leakage, degraded
intrinsic reflective capabilities, and late-stage training collapse [Kim
et al. (2026)](#bib.bib8); [Li et al. (2026c)](#bib.bib9).

Recent advancements attempt to mitigate this by anchoring optimization
to environment rewards for continuous magnitude adjustment [Yang et al.
(2026a)](#bib.bib3); [Li et al. (2026a)](#bib.bib1). Unfortunately, a
subtle limitation remains: because the privileged context narrows the
teacher’s output distribution onto specific oracle tokens, the teacher’s
probabilities for most student-generated tokens are systematically lower
than the student’s own. This causes the continuous multipliers to be
predominantly less than 1, dampening the primary reward signal.
Furthermore, the privileged information here is often simply the
directly provided ground truth; directly relying on it during training
is clearly inefficient. Consequently, such global distribution alignment
inevitably allows privileged information to implicitly leak into the
parameters, inducing late-stage training collapse.

To fully unlock self-distillation without these drawbacks, we propose
the Asymmetric Meta-Reflective Self-Distillation (AMR-SD) framework,
which retains the reward-anchoring principle of [Yang et al.
(2026a)](#bib.bib3) while replacing continuous scaling with an
asymmetric, ReLU-gated threshold ($`\tau`$), powered by a novel metric:
Causal Information Gain (CIG). To mitigate direct oracle-solution
leakage, AMR-SD operates as a reflection-mediated self-training loop.
Instead of exposing the teacher to raw ground-truth solutions during
token rescoring, we enforce a Meta-Reflection phase: the model generates
an encouraging \<hint\> for successful trajectories or a targeted
\<critique\> for failed trajectories, using verifier-approved peer
rollouts when available, which then serve as the conditioning context
for the teacher.

Crucially, to overcome the signal dampening inherent in continuous
scaling, CIG introduces an asymmetric, threshold-gated filtering
mechanism. Rather than diluting the reward by modulating every token,
this mechanism acts as a strict gatekeeper: it preserves the baseline
environmental reward intact by default, triggering sparse, targeted
adjustments only when the Socratic teacher identifies a highly confident
divergence from the student. This approach effectively filters out
trivial distributional noise, delivering precise token-level credit
assignment without compromising the overall strength of the base
reinforcement signal.

We emphasize that AMR-SD does not entirely discard privileged
information (e.g., verifier outcomes, peer rollouts, or reference
answers). Instead, it prevents the token-rescoring teacher from directly
seeing raw oracle traces. Diagnostic sources are first compressed into
concise natural-language reflections, acting as a low-bandwidth
bottleneck. This mitigates over-conditioned teacher distributions and
answer leakage while preserving essential token-level guidance for
credit assignment.

Our main contributions are threefold:

- •
  We introduce Meta-Reflection, prompting the model to generate Socratic
  self-teaching targets (hint / critique) from verifier outcomes,
  on-policy peer rollouts, or reference-assisted diagnostic signals when
  available. This reflection-mediated paradigm does not remove
  privileged information, but introduces a low-bandwidth bottleneck
  between diagnostic sources and token-level rescoring, thereby reducing
  direct oracle-trace conditioning and improving calibration of
  token-level credit signals.
- •
  We design CIG as a threshold-gated (ReLU) advantage adjustment
  mechanism. Integrated with temporal annealing, it concentrates dense
  supervision during early learning and smoothly shifts to unadulterated
  environmental rewards, ensuring rapid early alignment and long-horizon
  stability.
- •
  Building upon these mechanisms, we propose the AMR-SD framework.
  Extensive experiments across scientific, mathematical, and tool-use
  benchmarks demonstrate that AMR-SD outperforms existing baselines,
  achieving robust long-horizon stability and successfully preventing
  the late-stage training collapse.

## 2 Related Work and Background

#### RL with Verifiable Rewards and GRPO.

Proximal Policy Optimization [Schulman et al. (2017)](#bib.bib14)
established the foundation for RLVR-based LLM alignment [Yu et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib28); [Wu et al. (2025)](#bib.bib27). Recent works have
further analyzed the properties of verifiable reward signals [Wen et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib6); [Lu et al. (2026)](#bib.bib16); [Lin et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib17). To optimize the policy under sparse rewards without
a separate value network, GRPO [Guo et al. (2025)](#bib.bib4) estimates
advantages via group baseline normalization. For a given prompt $`x`$,
the policy samples $`G`$ independent trajectories. The advantage for the
$`i`$-th trajectory is calculated as
$`A_{i}=(r_{i}-\mu_{\text{group}})/(\sigma_{\text{group}}+\varepsilon)`$,
where $`\mu_{\text{group}}`$ and $`\sigma_{\text{group}}`$ are the mean
and standard deviation of the $`G`$ rewards.

Although subsequent systems such as DAPO [Yu et al. (2026)](#bib.bib5)
improve training stability, GRPO’s advantage estimates are known to be
biased [Yang et al. (2026b)](#bib.bib21). More critically, applying a
uniform scalar advantage $`A_{i}`$ to every token creates a severe
credit-assignment bottleneck [Yang et al. (2026b)](#bib.bib21); [Li et
al. (2026d)](#bib.bib26); [Xie et al. (2025)](#bib.bib25); [Li et al.
(2026b)](#bib.bib24). Some works attempt to address this through
uncertainty-aware advantage shaping [Xie et al. (2025)](#bib.bib25),
outcome-grounded advantage reshaping [Li et al. (2026d)](#bib.bib26),
and token-level policy gradient redesign for tool use [Lin et al.
(2025a)](#bib.bib22); [Lin et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib23); [Lin et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib17), yet fine-grained credit assignment remains
challenging.

#### On-Policy (Self-)Distillation.

To provide denser, token-level supervision, On-Policy Distillation
(OPD) [Agarwal et al. (2024)](#bib.bib7) trains a student on its own
online rollouts evaluated by a stronger external teacher (e.g.,
MiMo [Xiao et al. (2026)](#bib.bib13), Kimi [Team et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib15)). However, maintaining an external teacher imposes
substantial computational overhead. To eliminate this dependency,
On-Policy Self-Distillation [Zhao et al. (2026)](#bib.bib10); [Hübotter
et al. (2026)](#bib.bib2); [Shenfeld et al. (2026)](#bib.bib30); [Zhang
et al. (2026)](#bib.bib29) uses the model itself as the teacher. In this
paradigm, the active student policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$ generates
trajectories, and the exact same model, detached via a stop-gradient
operator ($`\pi_{\theta_{\text{sg}}}`$), acts as the teacher conditioned
on privileged information $`c`$.

Despite its efficiency, prior work [Kim et al. (2026)](#bib.bib8); [Li
et al. (2026c)](#bib.bib9) identifies that directly aligning the student
to these conditional log-likelihoods introduces privileged information
leakage and late-stage collapse. Recent methods [Yang et al.
(2026a)](#bib.bib3); [Li et al. (2026a)](#bib.bib1) attempt to stabilize
training by anchoring to environment rewards and using the teacher only
for continuous magnitude adjustment. Yet, their continuous scaling
predominantly dampens the overall learning signal. Our AMR-SD framework
resolves these issues via autonomous Meta-Reflection and a ReLU-gated
threshold, achieving sparse, unbiased token-level credit assignment
without external dependencies.

Input: Active policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$, Dataset $`\mathcal{D}`$;
Hyperparameters: $`\lambda,\gamma\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}`$, $`\tau\geq 0`$,
$`\kappa>0`$, $`T_{\text{decay}}\in\mathbb{N}`$

$`\theta_{\text{sg}}\leftarrow\theta_{\text{old}}`$ // Frozen old policy
and stop-gradient teacher

decoding // Teacher conditional and Student unconditional scores

19:

## 3 Method

We introduce the AMR-SD framework. Unlike standard sequence-level RL
which broadcasts a uniform advantage to all tokens, AMR-SD resolves the
spatial credit-assignment bottleneck by dynamically mapping the
sequence-level GRPO advantage into a dense, state-action specific
tensor.

Formally, we model the language generation process as a MDP defined by
the tuple $`(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P},\mathcal{R})`$. Let the
state $`s_{t}=(x,y_{<t})\in\mathcal{S}`$ denote the prompt and the
generated prefix, and the action $`a_{t}=y_{t}\in\mathcal{A}`$ represent
the current token. To construct a precise token-level advantage
$`\widehat{A}_{i,t}`$ without suffering from the information leakage
inherent in traditional self-distillation, our framework operates in
three sequential phases: Socratic Rescoring via Meta-Reflection, CIG
quantification, and Asymmetric Modulation.The full procedure is
summarized in
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ On-Policy (Self-)Distillation. ‣ 2 Related Work and Background ‣ AMR-SD: Asymmetric Meta-Reflective Self-Distillation for Token-Level Credit Assignment").

### 3.1 Socratic Rescoring via Meta-Reflection

To construct a dense reward signal without human annotation, we
formalize a Meta-Reflection mechanism that transitions the stop-gradient
policy $`\pi_{\theta_{\text{sg}}}`$ into a conditional Socratic
evaluator. Let $`\mathcal{C}`$ be the latent space of natural language
reflections. We define a discrete conditional mapping function
$`f_{\text{reflect}}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}^{T}\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathcal{C}`$
governed by the signum of the empirical advantage:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\begin{split}c_{i}&=f_{\text{reflect}}(x,y_{i},\text{sgn}(A_{i}))\\
&=\mathbb{I}_{\{A_{i}\geq 0\}}\cdot c_{\text{hint}}+\mathbb{I}_{\{A_{i}<0\}}\cdot c_{\text{critique}}\end{split}
``` |  | (1) |

where $`\mathbb{I}_{\{\cdot\}}`$ denotes the indicator function. The
hint reflection $`c_{\text{hint}}`$ extracts latent reasoning
trajectories for successful rollouts, while the critique reflection
$`c_{\text{critique}}`$ isolates logical or syntactic divergences in
failed ones.

Crucially, the Meta-Reflection phase is executed in-situ by the current
student policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$ itself. By generating hints and
critiques as intermediate Socratic reflections, AMR-SD does not expose
the rescoring teacher to raw oracle answers or full ground-truth
reasoning traces. Instead, outcome information is first compressed into
concise, structured natural-language guidance. This lower-bandwidth
conditioning mitigates the over-conditioning and answer-leakage risks of
directly conditioning the teacher on oracle solutions, while still
providing token-level guidance for credit assignment.

The teacher model subsequently evaluates the trajectory via forced
decoding over the augmented context vectors
$`[x\oplus c_{i}\oplus y_{i}]`$. This operation yields a conditional
state-transition probability distribution, defined as
$`\pi_{\theta_{\text{sg}}}(a_{t}\mid s_{t},c_{i})`$. By injecting
$`c_{i}`$, we effectively break the standard autoregressive Markov
assumption, allowing the teacher to retrospectively assess action
$`a_{t}`$ given the terminal trajectory outcome encoded in $`c_{i}`$.

### 3.2 Causal Information Gain (CIG)

To quantify the granular contribution of each action, we introduce CIG.
From an information-theoretic perspective, CIG measures the pointwise
log-likelihood ratio between the context-aware Socratic teacher and the
student policy. For an action $`a_{t}`$ at state $`s_{t}`$, the raw CIG
is computed as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\text{CIG}}=\log\left(\frac{\pi_{\theta_{\text{sg}}}(a_{t}\mid s_{t},c_{i})}{\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})}\right)
``` |  | (2) |

A strictly positive $`\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\text{CIG}}`$ indicates that the
transition $`(s_{t},a_{t})`$ is assigned a low probability by the
student but a high likelihood by the informed teacher, signaling a
knowledge deficit. Conversely, $`\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\text{CIG}}<0`$
implies student over-confidence relative to the Socratic baseline.

To guarantee bounded Lipschitz continuity in the subsequent gradient
updates and mitigate numerical instability caused by the heavy-tailed
nature of KL-divergence, we apply a symmetric clamping operator to the
information gain:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widehat{\mathcal{I}}_{t}^{\text{CIG}}=\operatorname{clip}(\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\text{CIG}},-\kappa,\kappa)
``` |  | (3) |

where $`\kappa\in\mathbb{R}^{+}`$ defines the maximum allowed
informational deviation. Based on our empirical observations of the CIG
distribution (detailed in Appendix
[E](#A5 "Appendix E Detailed Analysis: CIG Token Value Distribution ‣ AMR-SD: Asymmetric Meta-Reflective Self-Distillation for Token-Level Credit Assignment")),
we constrain this bound to $`\kappa=5`$ to mitigate numerical
instability while preserving meaningful signals.

### 3.3 Asymmetric Token-Level Advantage Modulation

We integrate the localized CIG with the global trajectory objective
through a non-linear, asymmetric modulation scalar $`\Delta_{t}`$. The
asymmetry is mathematically parameterized to decouple the gradient flows
for positive and negative rollouts, utilizing a noise-filtering
threshold $`\tau\in\mathbb{R}^{+}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\begin{split}\Delta_{t}=\;&\mathbb{I}_{\{A_{i}\geq 0\}}\cdot\lambda_{\text{eff}}\max(0,\widehat{\mathcal{I}}_{t}^{\text{CIG}}-\tau)\\
&+\mathbb{I}_{\{A_{i}<0\}}\cdot\gamma_{\text{eff}}\max(0,-\widehat{\mathcal{I}}_{t}^{\text{CIG}}-\tau)\end{split}
``` |  | (4) |

This formulation ensures orthogonal gradient scaling:

- •
  Reward Amplification: When $`A_{i}\geq 0`$, $`\Delta_{t}`$
  monotonically increases only for actions where the student
  underperformed the teacher
  ($`\widehat{\mathcal{I}}_{t}^{\text{CIG}}>\tau`$).
- •
  Penalty Amplification: When $`A_{i}<0`$, $`\Delta_{t}`$ monotonically
  increases only for actions where the student was erroneously
  over-confident ($`\widehat{\mathcal{I}}_{t}^{\text{CIG}}<-\tau`$).

The refined, token-level advantage tensor is thus expressed as a
multiplicative modulation of the original baseline:

|     |                                                       |     |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \widehat{A}_{i,t}=A_{i}\cdot\left(1+\Delta_{t}\right)
       ```                                                    |     | (5) |

#### Temporal Annealing Schedule

In late training stages, self-distillation encounters two bottlenecks.
First, reflection quality degrades: hints become redundant for
internalized reasoning, and residual errors become too complex for
accurate critiques. Second, the teacher reaches its intrinsic capability
ceiling, losing the ability to provide meaningful CIG signals to an
already highly-optimized student. To prevent overfitting to these
depleted signals, a linear temporal decay smoothly shifts the
optimization entirely to the pure environmental reward:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\{\lambda_{\text{eff}},\gamma_{\text{eff}}\}=\{\lambda,\gamma\}\cdot\max\left(0,1-\frac{t_{\text{global}}}{T_{\text{decay}}}\right)
``` |  | (6) |

where $`t_{\text{global}}`$ is current optimization step.

### 3.4 Optimization Objective

The student policy parameters $`\theta`$ are optimized by maximizing a
modified PPO clipped surrogate objective. We substitute the standard
trajectory advantage with our dense estimator $`\widehat{A}_{i,t}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\text{AMR-SD}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},y\sim\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}}\Bigg[\frac{1}{T_{i}}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{i}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{clip}}(\theta,t)\Bigg]
``` |  | (7) |

where the clipped surrogate term is defined as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\text{clip}}(\theta,t)=\min\Big(&\rho_{t}(\theta)\widehat{A}_{i,t},\\
&\text{clip}(\rho_{t}(\theta),1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon)\widehat{A}_{i,t}\Big)\end{split}
``` |  | (8) |

and the importance sampling ratio is
$`\rho_{t}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})}`$.
The gradient $`\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{AMR-SD}}(\theta)`$ now
incorporates both global trajectory optimality and precise token-level
informational corrections.

## 4 Experiment

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

We evaluate AMR-SD on: (1) Scientific Reasoning & Tool Use using
SciKnowEval [Feng et al. (2024)](#bib.bib11) and ToolAlpaca [Tang et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib12); (2) Mathematical Reasoning using DAPO-Math-17k [Yu
et al. (2026)](#bib.bib5) and benchmarks AIME 24/25, AMC 23, and HMMT.
Base models are Qwen3-8B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [Yang et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib19); [Bai et al. (2023)](#bib.bib18). We compare against
GRPO, SDPO, and RLSD. Models are trained via verl [Sheng et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib20) ($`G=8`$, $`T_{\text{decay}}=50`$). All tracks are
evaluated using acc@16, with scientific and tool-use tasks reported at
steps 15 and 75 to monitor stability. See Appendix
[D](#A4 "Appendix D Hyperparameters and Implementation Details ‣ AMR-SD: Asymmetric Meta-Reflective Self-Distillation for Token-Level Credit Assignment")
for data splits, hyperparameters details.

#### Scientific Reasoning and Tool Use.

We evaluate AMR-SD on the SciKnowEval benchmark across four scientific
disciplines (Chemistry, Physics, Biology, and Materials Science) as well
as a Tool Use task, using two backbone models: Qwen3-8B and
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Main Result ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ AMR-SD: Asymmetric Meta-Reflective Self-Distillation for Token-Level Credit Assignment")).
Across both backbones, all training methods substantially improve over
the untrained baselines, confirming that reinforcement learning provides
a consistent benefit for scientific reasoning. At final convergence
(step 75), AMR-SD achieves the strongest or near-strongest performance
in the majority of categories. Most significantly, AMR-SD attains the
highest Biology scores on both backbones by a substantial margin: 63.7
on Qwen3-8B and 66.4 on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, surpassing GRPO by
approximately 3.2 and 18.2 percentage points respectively, and exceeding
RLSD by roughly 7.2 and 11.8 percentage points. On Physics and Materials
Science, AMR-SD similarly reaches competitive or best-in-class scores at
step 75—79.7 on Physics and 80.3 on Materials for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct,
the highest figures among all methods in both categories. These results
suggest that the token-level credit assignment provided by the CIG
mechanism enables more reliable generalisation across diverse scientific
domains compared to trajectory-level or coarser reward signals.

#### Convergence Dynamics.

A notable pattern across both backbones is the distinct convergence
profile of AMR-SD relative to competing methods
(Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.2 Main Result ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ AMR-SD: Asymmetric Meta-Reflective Self-Distillation for Token-Level Credit Assignment")).
At the early checkpoint, AMR-SD frequently lags behind baseline methods
that aggressively exploit early reward signals. For instance, on the
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct Tool Use task, AMR-SD scores 61.0 at step 15,
trailing both GRPO (61.6) and RLSD (63.3). Similarly, on Qwen3-8B
Chemistry, AMR-SD (65.0) lags noticeably behind SDPO (69.2) and RLSD
(66.3). However, by step 75, these early gaps are closed or reversed,
with AMR-SD achieving the best or near-best scores in most categories on
both backbones. By contrast, RLSD exhibits early gains that subsequently
plateau or regress; its Biology score on Qwen3-8B improves only to 56.5
at step 75—well below AMR-SD’s 63.7. SDPO demonstrates the most
pronounced instability, suffering severe performance degradation on both
backbones and being excluded entirely from the step-75 Tool Use
evaluation due to severe policy collapse. These dynamics indicate that
AMR-SD’s fine-grained credit assignment trades off faster initial
convergence for more stable and ultimately superior long-run
optimization.

#### Mathematical Reasoning.

To assess generalisation beyond scientific knowledge tasks, we further
evaluate AMR-SD on four mathematical competition benchmarks—AIME24,
AIME25, AMC23, and HMMT—using Qwen3-8B in thinking
mode (Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Main Result ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ AMR-SD: Asymmetric Meta-Reflective Self-Distillation for Token-Level Credit Assignment")).
AMR-SD achieves the best performance on every individual benchmark and
the highest average score of 62.7, compared to 60.3 for GRPO (+2.4
points) and 57.2 for RLSD (+5.5 points). The gains are particularly
pronounced on the most challenging benchmarks: 69.6 on AIME24 (vs. 66.7
for GRPO), 55.2 on AIME25 (vs. 53.1), and 34.6 on HMMT (vs. 31.7).
Notably, RLSD shows constrained optimization efficiency on harder
problems, scoring 27.6 on HMMT and 47.3 on AIME25. This indicates that
directly using raw ground-truth solutions as privileged information
introduces a distributional shift that makes the resulting reward signal
insufficiently discriminative for complex multi-step reasoning.

Furthermore, we provide deeper analyses of optimization stability and
generation dynamics in Appendices
[C](#A3 "Appendix C Training Dynamics on Mathematical Reasoning ‣ AMR-SD: Asymmetric Meta-Reflective Self-Distillation for Token-Level Credit Assignment")
and
[F](#A6 "Appendix F Analysis of Reflection Capabilities and Reasoning Efficiency ‣ AMR-SD: Asymmetric Meta-Reflective Self-Distillation for Token-Level Credit Assignment").
As shown, while standard continuous self-distillation methods like RLSD
exhibit late-stage performance fluctuations and compressed reflection
behavior due to direct answer exposure, AMR-SD maintains a stable,
monotonically improving reward signal. Crucially, AMR-SD improves
reasoning efficiency by reducing unnecessary verbosity while
successfully preserving critical cognitive explorations. This confirms
that introducing a reflection bottleneck successfully mitigates the
vulnerabilities inherent in direct answer conditioning, effectively
translating training stability to superior out-of-domain accuracy.

### 4.3 Analysis: Quality of Meta-Reflections

The efficacy of AMR-SD hinges on the quality of self-generated
reflections, as they directly calibrate the CIG-based advantage
modulation. A precise reflection concentrates the learning signal on
semantically informative tokens, whereas a vague or factually incorrect
one risks propagating miscalibrated supervision.

Qualitative analysis of sampled reflections from SciKnowEval and
DAPO-Math-17k rollouts reveals two consistent patterns. First, hints for
successful trajectories effectively distill latent core principles
rather than merely repeating the answer path. Second, critiques for
failed trajectories demonstrate precise fault localization, diagnosing
root causes and reframing them in a positive, prospective manner. This
"positive-framing" is crucial; as the critique is prepended to the
teacher’s forward pass, it provides constructive guidance that enables
the model to resolve the underlying reasoning divergence. Detailed
representative examples of these Socratic targets are provided in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Reflection Sample ‣ AMR-SD: Asymmetric Meta-Reflective Self-Distillation for Token-Level Credit Assignment").

### 4.4 Ablation Study

To disentangle the contribution of each component in AMR-SD, we conduct
an ablation study on a combined SciKnowEval benchmark, mixing Chemistry,
Physics, Biology, and Materials Science for both training and
evaluation. All variants are trained on Qwen3-8B and evaluated using
Acc@16. Results are reported in
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.4 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ AMR-SD: Asymmetric Meta-Reflective Self-Distillation for Token-Level Credit Assignment").

| Method Setting                          | Acc@16 |
|-----------------------------------------|--------|
| Qwen3-8B                                | 46.9   |
| AMR-SD(Full)                            | 74.3   |
| \+ w/o Meta-Reflection                  | 70.5   |
| \+ w/o CIG Threshold ($`\tau`$)         | 72.0   |
| \+ w/o CIG Asymmetric ReLU and $`\tau`$ | 71.3   |
| \+ w/o Temporal Annealing               | 70.6   |

Table 3: Ablation study of the AMR-SD framework on Qwen3-8B (Acc@16).
Results validate the necessity of Meta-Reflection, the CIG threshold
($`\tau`$), asymmetric ReLU gating, and temporal annealing.

#### Effect of Meta-Reflection.

In this ablation variant, we replace the model’s self-generated
meta-reflection with the ground-truth solution directly as the teacher’s
conditioning context. Performance drops from 74.3 to 70.5, a reduction
of 3.8 points. This result reveals a counterintuitive finding: injecting
privileged ground-truth information as the conditioning signal is
strictly inferior to the model’s own Socratic self-reflection. The
underlying cause lies in the information asymmetry problem: when the
teacher is conditioned on the ground-truth answer, its token probability
distribution presupposes information unavailable to the student,
creating a fundamental distributional gap that inflates CIG estimates
and induces miscalibrated advantage modulation. By contrast,
self-generated hints and critiques share the same information boundary
as the student policy, yielding better-calibrated CIG signals and more
precise gradient interventions.

#### Effect of the ReLU Threshold $`\tau`$.

Removing the margin $`\tau`$ while retaining the ReLU gate yields 72.0,
surpassing the no-reflection baseline but falling 2.3 points below the
full model. The threshold enforces sparsity: without it, low-magnitude
CIG signals that correspond to distributional noise rather than genuine
knowledge deficits are allowed to modulate the advantage, diluting
gradient quality. Further ablating the ReLU gate itself reduces accuracy
to 71.3. In this setting, the mechanism loses its asymmetric directional
filtering. Without the gate, “counter-directional” signals—such as
positive CIG in a failed rollout or negative CIG in a successful one—can
freely offset the intended advantage modulation, partially undermining
the primary reward signal. These two ablations validate that gate and
margin are necessary for robust, noise-resistant, and
directionally-aware credit assignment.

#### Effect of Temporal Annealing.

Disabling the decay schedule reduces performance to 70.6. In late
training stages, as the student policy becomes highly optimized, its
residual errors become increasingly complex. This not only degrades
self-reflection quality but also exhausts the teacher model’s inherent
capacity to provide reliable token-level guidance. Without annealing,
persistent distillation forces the policy to learn from these noisy,
depleted signals. Temporal annealing mitigates this by smoothly shifting
the optimization focus entirely to the pure environmental reward.

#### Full Model.

The complete AMR-SD configuration achieves 74.3, demonstrating that all
four components are mutually reinforcing rather than individually
redundant.

### 4.5 Analysis: CIG Token Value Distribution

As detailed in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Detailed Analysis: CIG Token Value Distribution ‣ AMR-SD: Asymmetric Meta-Reflective Self-Distillation for Token-Level Credit Assignment"),
the empirical distribution of non-zero CIG values across $`n=50{,}000`$
sampled tokens exhibits a pronounced left skew, with the bulk of mass
concentrated in the interval $`[-1,0]`$ and a peak just below zero. This
shape is a direct consequence of the teacher’s privileged information.
When the teacher model conditions on the meta-reflection, its output
distribution is recalibrated, systematically driving the bulk of CIG
values below zero.

The asymmetry has a direct consequence for hyperparameter selection.
Because tokens satisfying the critique condition vastly outnumber those
satisfying the hint condition (as shown in the appendix), setting
$`\lambda>\gamma`$ compensates for this imbalance by up-weighting the
sparser positive-CIG tokens. The result is a more balanced effective
gradient that leverages both signals without allowing either to
overwhelm the other.

## 5 Conclusion

In this paper, we introduced AMR-SD to resolve the token-level
credit-assignment bottleneck in RLVR. To overcome the privileged
information leakage and signal dampening inherent in standard
self-distillation, AMR-SD employs an autonomous Meta-Reflection phase to
generate Socratic hints and critiques. We formalized CIG with an
asymmetric, ReLU-gated threshold to translate these reflections into
sparse, precise token-level interventions, strictly preserving the base
environmental reward. Extensive experiments across scientific
(SciKnowEval), mathematical (AIME, AMC, HMMT), and tool-use (ToolAlpaca)
benchmarks demonstrate that AMR-SD significantly outperforms
state-of-the-art baselines. By effectively filtering distributional
noise and utilizing temporal annealing, our framework guarantees
long-horizon stability and avoids late-stage training collapse,
providing a highly robust, scalable solution for aligning large language
models on complex reasoning and agentic tasks.

## Limitations

Despite the strong empirical results, AMR-SD has two notable
limitations.

#### Dependence on Reflection Quality.

The effectiveness of the CIG mechanism is fundamentally contingent on
the quality of the self-generated meta-reflections. When the base model
lacks sufficient introspective capability, the produced hints and
critiques tend to be vague or factually miscalibrated, propagating
corrupted supervision signals through the CIG modulation and ultimately
degrading performance. This manifests most clearly in mathematical
reasoning tasks: on weaker or non-thinking-mode models such as
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B with enable_thinking=False, the
reflection quality is insufficient to yield reliable CIG signals, and
the method fails to outperform the GRPO baseline. AMR-SD is therefore
most effective when deployed on models with strong chain-of-thought or
self-evaluation capabilities.

#### Inference Overhead from Meta-Reflection Generation.

The meta-reflection phase introduces an additional autoregressive
generation step per trajectory during training rollouts. Although this
overhead is bounded by the reflection budget (capped at 4096 tokens for
SciKnowEval and 16384 tokens for math), it nonetheless increases the
wall-clock time per training iteration relative to standard GRPO or
RLSD. However, this computational overhead is highly manageable in
practice. Empirically, our method generally maintains a training speed
of at least 80% (e.g., in the mathematical reasoning task, during the
first 50 steps before method degeneration, GRPO and RLSD took 18 hours,
whereas AMR-SD took 22 hours) compared to standard GRPO. For severely
resource-constrained settings, this latency may still be a practical
concern, and future work could explore lightweight reflection
distillation or early-exit strategies to further reduce this cost.

## Appendix C Training Dynamics on Mathematical Reasoning

In this section, we provide a detailed visualization of the training
dynamics using the Qwen3-8B model with thinking mode enabled.
Figure [3](#A3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Appendix C Training Dynamics on Mathematical Reasoning ‣ AMR-SD: Asymmetric Meta-Reflective Self-Distillation for Token-Level Credit Assignment")
tracks the evaluation accuracy (acc@16) on the out-of-domain AIME 2024
benchmark alongside the average training reward on the DAPO-Math-17k
dataset over 150 training steps.

We observe distinct convergence profiles among the evaluated methods.
While GRPO demonstrates stable optimization in training reward, its
evaluation accuracy quickly plateaus, indicating a generalization
bottleneck. Conversely, RLSD experiences a brief initial surge but
suffers a severe performance collapse precisely as the distillation
signal anneals and diminishes (after step 50). Crucially, the right
panel reveals that this evaluation collapse is tightly correlated with a
sharp degradation in training reward. This indicates that RLSD’s
continuous scaling mechanism during the early stages fails to filter out
distributional noise, injecting uncalibrated signals that drive the
policy into a brittle, overfitted state. Once the distillation guidance
is fully decayed, this corrupted policy is unable to sustain
optimization under the pure environmental reward, leading to a severe
optimization collapse.

In contrast, AMR-SD (aided by the CIG threshold and temporal annealing)
achieves a highly stable and continuously improving training reward.
More importantly, it successfully translates this internal optimization
stability into the highest peak evaluation accuracy on AIME 2024. This
confirms that our fine-grained, token-level credit assignment not only
stabilizes the RL training process but also significantly enhances the
model’s true generalization capacity for complex mathematical reasoning.

Figure 3: Training dynamics using Qwen3-8B in thinking mode. Left:
Evaluation accuracy (acc@16) on the AIME 2024 benchmark over 150
training steps. AMR-SD maintains stable, state-of-the-art performance,
whereas RLSD suffers from a severe performance collapse post-annealing.
Right: Average training reward on the DAPO-Math-17k dataset. The
evaluation collapse of RLSD is accompanied by a sharp degradation in
training reward, indicating an intrinsic optimization failure. AMR-SD,
by contrast, maintains stable reward growth, successfully bridging
in-domain optimization with out-of-domain generalization.

## Appendix D Hyperparameters and Implementation Details

#### Datasets and Tasks.

We evaluate AMR-SD on two complementary tracks. For scientific knowledge
reasoning and agentic capabilities, we adopt the SciKnowEval
benchmark [Feng et al. (2024)](#bib.bib11), spanning four domains
(Chemistry, Physics, Biology, and Materials Science), alongside a
dedicated Tool Use benchmark [Tang et al. (2023)](#bib.bib12). We follow
exactly the training and test splits used in SDPO, enabling a direct and
fair comparison. For mathematical reasoning, we train on the
preprocessed DAPO-Math-17k dataset [Yu et al. (2026)](#bib.bib5) and
evaluate on four standard benchmarks: AIME 2024, AIME 2025, AMC 2023,
and HMMT.

#### Base Models and Baselines.

We conduct experiments on two instruction-tuned base models: Qwen3-8B
and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [Yang et al. (2025)](#bib.bib19); [Bai et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib18). For all SciKnowEval and Tool Use experiments, we
evaluate on both models with the thinking mode disabled
(enable_thinking=False) to ensure a controlled comparison. Conversely,
for mathematical reasoning, we exclusively employ Qwen3-8B with the
thinking mode enabled (enable_thinking=True). We compare AMR-SD against
the following baselines: (1) the pretrained base model without any RL
fine-tuning; (2) GRPO, the standard sequence-level policy gradient
baseline; (3) SDPO, a representative on-policy self-distillation method;
and (4) RLSD, a state-of-the-art reward-anchored magnitude-adjustment
approach. Notably, SDPO is excluded from the mathematical reasoning
evaluation due to its severe performance degradation in this domain.

#### Training Details.

All models are trained using the verl framework [Sheng et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib20) with FSDP distributed training and vLLM-accelerated
rollout generation. Regarding task allocation and hardware, the
mathematical reasoning model is trained on the preprocessed
DAPO-Math-17k dataset. In contrast, the four domains of SciKnowEval and
the Tool Use task are trained independently for each specific task. For
each training prompt, we sample $`G=8`$ independent trajectories at
temperature $`1.0`$ with top-$`p=1.0`$. The actor is optimized with
AdamW at a learning rate of $`1\times 10^{-6}`$, with a training batch
size of 256 for SciKnowEval and Tool Use, and 512 for math. The maximum
prompt and response lengths are set to 1024 and 2048 tokens respectively
for SciKnowEval and Tool Use, and 2048 and 16384 tokens for math.
Following the training configuration of RLSD, we set the temporal
annealing horizon $`T_{\mathrm{decay}}=50`$ steps, after which the
objective degenerates smoothly to standard GRPO. The meta-reflection
generation budget is capped at 4096 tokens for SciKnowEval and 16384
tokens for math.

Crucially, for the Socratic evaluator $`\pi_{\theta_{\text{sg}}}`$, we
employ a direct evaluation strategy rather than a lagging moving
average. During training, the evaluation weights $`\theta_{\text{sg}}`$
are strictly synchronized with the active policy $`\theta`$ at every
step ($`\theta_{\text{sg}}=\text{stop\_gradient}(\theta)`$). This design
eliminates the need for additional hyperparameter tuning (e.g., EMA
decay rates) while ensuring the evaluator remains perfectly coupled with
the student’s progression. Operating solely in inference mode without
gradient tracking, $`\pi_{\theta_{\text{sg}}}`$ provides a stable,
zero-lag baseline for CIG estimation.

#### Hyperparameter Configurations.

To account for the highly skewed empirical distribution of CIG values
(as detailed in Appendix
[E](#A5 "Appendix E Detailed Analysis: CIG Token Value Distribution ‣ AMR-SD: Asymmetric Meta-Reflective Self-Distillation for Token-Level Credit Assignment")),
we employ asymmetric modulation coefficients. Specifically, the reward
amplification coefficient is set to $`\lambda=0.2`$, while the penalty
amplification coefficient is set to $`\gamma=0.1`$. This configuration
effectively up-weights the sparser positive-CIG tokens, ensuring a
balanced gradient signal that leverages both hint bonuses and critique
penalties.

#### Evaluation Protocol.

During evaluation, we strictly control the generation boundaries to
match the distinct requirements of each track. For SciKnowEval and the
Tool Use benchmark, we set the maximum generation length to 2048 tokens.
We report per-domain accuracy at two training checkpoints—step 15 and
step 75—to assess both early convergence and final performance, with
validation performed every 5 training steps. For mathematical reasoning,
we expand the maximum generation length to 16384 tokens to accommodate
extended and complex reasoning chains. Performance is evaluated using
acc@16, computed as the average accuracy over 16 independently sampled
rollouts per problem at temperature $`1.0`$, across AIME 2024, AIME
2025, AMC 2023, and HMMT.

## Appendix E Detailed Analysis: CIG Token Value Distribution

This section provides the visual empirical distribution and a detailed
theoretical analysis of the Causal Information Gain (CIG) values
discussed in Section 4.5 of the main text.

![Refer to caption](2605.18529v1/figure/token_cig_distribution.png)

Figure 4: Empirical distribution of non-zero CIG values. The prominent
left skew (peaking just below zero) is caused by the teacher’s
conditioning on privileged information. This intrinsic asymmetry
necessitates differential scaling coefficients ($`\lambda>\gamma`$) to
balance penalties and bonuses.

As presented in
Figure [4](#A5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Appendix E Detailed Analysis: CIG Token Value Distribution ‣ AMR-SD: Asymmetric Meta-Reflective Self-Distillation for Token-Level Credit Assignment"),
the empirical distribution of non-zero CIG values across $`n=50{,}000`$
sampled tokens exhibits a pronounced left skew, with the bulk of mass
concentrated in the interval $`[-1,0]`$ and a peak just below zero. This
shape is a direct consequence of the teacher’s privileged information.

When the teacher model conditions on the meta-reflection—a hint or
critique unavailable to the student—its output distribution is
recalibrated: probability mass shifts toward alternative continuations,
and by the softmax normalization constraint, the probability assigned to
the token actually produced by the student decreases. This effect is
systematic and occurs across both correct and incorrect trajectories,
driving the bulk of CIG values below zero.

The asymmetry has a direct consequence for hyperparameter selection.
Recall that the hint bonus activates on correct trajectories when
$`\mathrm{CIG}_{t}>\tau`$, while the critique penalty activates on wrong
trajectories when $`-\mathrm{CIG}_{t}>\tau`$. As
Figure [4](#A5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Appendix E Detailed Analysis: CIG Token Value Distribution ‣ AMR-SD: Asymmetric Meta-Reflective Self-Distillation for Token-Level Credit Assignment")
shows, the negative tail is substantially heavier: tokens satisfying the
critique condition vastly outnumber those satisfying the hint condition.
If $`\lambda=\gamma`$, the aggregate gradient signal would be dominated
by critique penalties, suppressing the learning contribution from hint
bonuses. Setting $`\lambda>\gamma`$ compensates for this imbalance by
up-weighting the sparser positive-CIG tokens. The result is a more
balanced effective gradient that leverages both the reinforcement of
teacher-preferred tokens on correct trajectories and the attenuation of
teacher-opposed tokens on wrong ones, without allowing either signal to
overwhelm the other.

## Appendix F Analysis of Reflection Capabilities and Reasoning Efficiency

#### Motivation.

While our Asymmetric Meta-Reflective Self-Distillation (AMR-SD)
framework significantly improves accuracy and reasoning efficiency, a
critical concern in On-Policy Distillation is whether the dense
supervision alters the model’s intrinsic ability to explore and reflect.
Standard self-distillation often forces the student to mimic an
oracle-conditioned teacher. When this teacher is directly exposed to
ground-truth answers, it can induce over-alignment and restrict natural
trial-and-error, resulting in more short-sighted generation. To
investigate this, we analyze the generation dynamics of different
alignment strategies by quantifying their reflection capabilities.

#### Methodology.

We sample $`n=480`$ evaluation traces from the AIME 24 benchmark. To
measure the degree of internal deliberation, we track the frequency of
ten explicit reflection and self-correction markers (e.g., Wait, Maybe,
Check, Alternatively, Seems, Might, Hmm, Perhaps, Actually, Likely,
following [Kim et al., 2026](#bib.bib8)) across four distinct models:
the Base model (Qwen3-8B), standard GRPO, RLSD, and our proposed AMR-SD.

| Method                                | Total Count | Avg. per Trace |
|---------------------------------------|-------------|----------------|
| Base Model (Qwen3-8B)                 | 67,632      | 140.90         |
| GRPO [Guo et al. (2025)](#bib.bib4)   | 56,432      | 117.57         |
| RLSD [Yang et al. (2026a)](#bib.bib3) | 35,324      | 73.59          |
| AMR-SD (Ours)                         | 50,553      | 105.32         |

Table 4: Frequency of key reflection and self-correction markers across
480 AIME 24 evaluation traces. AMR-SD successfully reduces the excessive
verbosity of the base model while preserving the core reflection
capabilities that are otherwise compressed in direct answer-conditioned
self-distillation.

#### Results and Discussion.

As shown in
Table [4](#A6.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Methodology. ‣ Appendix F Analysis of Reflection Capabilities and Reasoning Efficiency ‣ AMR-SD: Asymmetric Meta-Reflective Self-Distillation for Token-Level Credit Assignment"),
the Base model exhibits extreme verbosity (140.90 markers per trace),
often over-thinking without converging to a solution. While GRPO reduces
some redundancy (117.57), it still relies heavily on prolonged
generation to maximize rewards.

Crucially, standard RLSD experiences a shift in reflection markers,
dropping to an average of 73.59 per trace. This strongly confirms that
previous self-distillation methods—which directly expose the
ground-truth answer as privileged information—tend to over-condition the
teacher’s distribution. Because the teacher already contains the
terminal answer explicitly, its rescored probability landscape
implicitly disincentivizes the student’s natural logical branching or
explicit trial-and-error attempts. Consequently, the model shifts
towards more accelerated, direct paths, compressing its long-horizon
exploration.

In contrast, our AMR-SD framework strikes an optimal balance,
maintaining a healthy reflection frequency of 105.32 markers per trace.
This "Goldilocks effect" is directly attributable to replacing direct
answer exposure with an information bottleneck (Meta-Reflection)
combined with the Asymmetric Causal Information Gain (CIG) threshold.
Rather than penalizing cognitive explorations, the asymmetric threshold
acts as a precise filter: it heavily penalizes blindly confident
deviations (baseless waffle) while tolerating and protecting valid
analytical trajectories (e.g., “Wait, alternatively…”). This
demonstrates that AMR-SD effectively enhances reasoning efficiency
without stripping the model of the crucial critical thinking
capabilities required for solving complex mathematical problems.
````
